clue.text: Package somehow goes around seemingly forever

indicators.note: the words go around the target, wrapping its letters inside the run of text across the word break

parts.note: the tail of the first word and the head of the second

explanation.surface: A parcel that seems to travel around the world for an eternity before it arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes around' reads as the parcel's journey, but it signals that the two words surround the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Waiting for ages is the idiom for a very long time, which feels as if it lasts without end.

clue.text: Goodwill shown by good people

parts.note: standard abbreviation for good
a race is a people, a group sharing descent

explanation.surface: Kindness displayed by decent folk.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace can mean favour or kindly disposition, as in being in someone's good graces.

clue.text: Players leaving? That's hilarious

parts.note: a side is a team of players
splitting is slang for leaving or departing

explanation.surface: Someone finds it hilarious that the players are walking off.
explanation.walkthrough: To split is informal for to leave, as in 'let's split'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something side-splitting makes you laugh so hard your ribs seem to burst, so it is extremely funny.

clue.text: Boy, it's, er, crazy being off the booze

indicators.note: something crazy is disordered, so the preceding letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the three short words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A hesitant speaker suggests that a lad going teetotal is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'er' reads as a stammer but contributes two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sobriety is the state of not drinking alcohol, so it names the condition of abstaining from drink.

clue.text: Amount of ice cream possibly in small shop

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a co-op is a cooperative store; the Co-op is a British supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A helping of ice cream sold in a little store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one piece inside another, but here it only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded ladleful of ice cream is called a scoop; 'possibly' signals this is one example of the word's uses.

clue.text: Money reduced the range

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the word that follows loses its final letter

parts.note: bread is slang for cash
taken as written

explanation.surface: A budget cut has narrowed the selection on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' sits after 'Money' as if it qualifies it, but it docks the E from 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Breadth is width or extent, so a wide range of things has great breadth.

clue.text: Match between countries is not a triennial, strangely

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the preceding letters are set out in an odd order

parts.note: all thirteen letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A sports fixture between nations is, oddly, not held every three years.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport, an international is a game played between teams representing two nations.

clue.text: Golden syrup topping for tasty new cereal

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so the next word's letters are remade in a different order
the topping of a word is its head, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the initial of tasty
the six letters of cereal rearranged

explanation.surface: A sweet syrup drizzled over a new breakfast cereal to make it tasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Golden syrup is a pale British treacle sold in tins.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain treacle covers syrups from refining sugar, and golden syrup is the pale variety of it.

clue.text: Good-looking workers love me!

parts.note: hands are manual workers, as in farmhands
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vain boast that labourers adore the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Handsome describes someone attractive in appearance, chiefly a man.

clue.text: Article primarily mentioning those people

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the initial of mentioning

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece that mainly talks about a certain group.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun refers to a group previously named, standing for those persons as an object.

clue.text: Arranges group drink

parts.note: a set is a group of things
to sup is to drink, especially in sips

explanation.surface: Someone organises a round of drinks for the gang.
explanation.definitionFit: To set something up is to organise or prepare it, the phrasal verb matching arranges.

clue.text: Member of family is upset with son

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A relative is distressed alongside her boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sis is the informal short form of sister, a female sibling within a household.

clue.text: Awful Conservative beginning to take lead

parts.note: dire means dreadful
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the initial of take

explanation.surface: A dreadful Tory starts to take charge of the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a noun here, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct people is to guide or steer them, which is what leading them means.

clue.text: Arrogant and shallow, needed to change

indicators.note: the letters are made to change their places, producing a different arrangement

parts.note: all thirteen letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A conceited, superficial person was told they had to change.
explanation.definitionFit: Being big-headed or conceited is the idiom, with an inflated sense of one's own importance.

clue.text: Loss of assets regularly hidden by regular payment

indicators.note: something hidden by another is enclosed within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a wage is a regular payment for work

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken starting from the first

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of assets

explanation.surface: Assets being lost, concealed through a regular salary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' and 'regular' sit close together but do different jobs: one picks letters, the other belongs to the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Wastage is the amount lost through waste or decline, so it means a reduction or loss.

clue.text: Each short afternoon nap is most convenient

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the nap word loses its last letter

parts.note: ea is the abbreviation for each, as on price tags
a siesta is an afternoon sleep

explanation.surface: A brief nap after lunch every day is the handiest thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Easiest is the superlative of easy, meaning requiring least effort, hence handiest of all.

clue.text: Stain interior of shed yearly

indicators.note: the inside of the run of text across the two words holds the letters needed

parts.note: the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone treats the inside of a garden hut with wood stain every year.
explanation.definitionFit: Stain and dye both describe colouring matter applied to wood or fabric, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Sparkling wine's found around the middle of Neive, currently

indicators.note: the wine is found surrounding the selected letter, enclosing it

parts.note: Asti is a sparkling Italian wine, plus the S of the possessive

indicators.note: the middle of a five-letter word is its third letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the centre letter of Neive

explanation.surface: Bubbly from the Piedmont village of Neive is being found at the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Neive is a village in Piedmont near Asti, which makes the wine look like the setting rather than wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in the present state of things, unchanged, which matches currently or at present.

clue.text: A gun for each person

parts.note: taken as written
piece is slang for a handgun

explanation.surface: A firearm handed out to every individual.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means to or for every one, as in costing a pound per item or individual.

clue.text: Extra publicity ultimately pleased the board

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement, a piece of publicity

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter of each of the following words is kept

parts.note: the final letters of the three words

explanation.surface: More advertising eventually satisfied the company directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' seems to modify 'pleased' alone, but it takes the tail of all three words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Something added is supplementary or additional, put on top of what was there, so it is extra.

clue.text: Top clubs, ahead of all others

indicators.note: being ahead of something places it first, so the first piece precedes the second

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit
the rest means everyone else

explanation.surface: Top golf or football clubs leading the whole field.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is the peak or summit of a hill or wave, the highest point.

clue.text: Government levy attached to one hire vehicle

parts.note: a tax is a levy charged by government
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A state charge added to a single rental car.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab is a car whose driver is paid to carry passengers, so it is a vehicle for hire.

clue.text: Threaten complete fury

parts.note: to complete something is to end it
fury is intense anger

explanation.surface: Someone menaces another with total rage.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger is to put at risk or imperil, which is what threatening something does.

clue.text: Stood by, we're told, carrying loads?

indicators.note: what we are told is heard rather than read, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

parts.note: stood by means remained in readiness

explanation.surface: Someone stood waiting while carrying heavy burdens.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a slightly loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weighted is burdened or loaded down with heavy material, so it bears a heavy load.

clue.text: In part, you're talking about holding everyone up, maybe?

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the concealed run is read backwards
only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone's chatter is making everyone wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talking about' reads as one phrase, but 'about' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving after the expected time keeps others waiting, so tardiness is one example of delaying a group; hence the question mark.
